questions.stem: What is the equation for Newton's Second Law?
questions.explanation: Newton's Second Law is F = ma, where F is the resultant force in newtons, m is mass in kg, and a is acceleration in m/s^2.

questions.stem: If the resultant force on an object is doubled while mass stays constant, the acceleration will:
questions.explanation: From F = ma, acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force. If force doubles and mass is constant, acceleration also doubles.

questions.stem: A resultant force of 600 N acts on a 200 kg object. What is the acceleration?
If the mass of an object is doubled while the force stays the same, the acceleration will:
questions.explanation: From F = ma, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. Doubling the mass while keeping force constant halves the acceleration.

questions.stem: In the equation F = ma, the F must be:

options.text: Any single force acting on the object
The resultant (net) force on the object

questions.explanation: The F in F = ma must be the resultant (net) force -- the vector sum of all forces acting on the object, not just any single force.

questions.stem: What force is needed to give a 5 kg mass an acceleration of 4 m/s^2?
questions.explanation: F = ma = 5 kg x 4 m/s^2 = 20 N.

questions.stem: One newton is defined as the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of:
questions.explanation: By definition, 1 N = 1 kg x 1 m/s^2. A force of 1 newton gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s^2.
